messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rajesh

Rajesh had been a paramedic for thirty-four years. He knew the weight of a stretcher, the smell of antiseptic, the particular silence that falls over a crew when they know they've done everything they can. On a Tuesday evening in March, responding to a chemical spill at an industrial facility thirty miles north of the city, he had learned what it meant to breathe poison. The warehouse had been poorly ventilated, the drums inadequately labeled. When he and his partner arrived, the acrid fumes were already thick in the air—something caustic and alien that burned his throat and made his eyes stream. He'd worked through it, as he always did, moving a contaminated worker to the decontamination area, stripping off his own gear afterward in the parking lot. By the next morning, his lungs felt scraped raw. Within seventy-two hours, he was in the hospital with chemical pneumonitis, struggling to breathe, certain he was dying. He recovered, physically. The doctors said he was lucky. But luck, Rajesh came to understand, was a relative thing.

Within weeks, the workplace had become a minefield. The smell of hand sanitizer in the ambulance station—something he'd never particularly noticed before—now sent his heart racing. The darkness of the equipment bay at night triggered a cascade of dread that made him grip the door frame. And the worst was the olfactory phantom: the smell of alcohol, which bore some chemical similarity to the fumes, would appear without warning—on a colleague's breath, in a cleaning solution, wafting from someone's hand sanitizer—and suddenly he was back in that warehouse, lungs burning, certain that this time he wouldn't survive it. Each trigger yanked him back into the full sensory nightmare, the terror as immediate as if the exposure were happening again.

The memories themselves had become unbearable. When he lay in bed at night and the memory surfaced, he was flooded with such overwhelming emotion that he had to get up, turn on every light, find something—anything—to do. He couldn't sit with it. The feeling was too large, too raw. So he began to structure his life around never being alone with his thoughts. He volunteered for extra shifts, filled his evenings with dinner parties and social gatherings, kept the television on constantly. His wife, Priya, initially supportive, began to notice that he couldn't sit through a meal without checking his phone, that he seemed almost frantic in his need for company. The rumination had started too—lying awake, running through the scenario obsessively, convinced that if he'd only arrived five minutes earlier, if he'd insisted on better ventilation checks, if he'd worn a different mask, none of this would have happened. The more he ruminated about how the event could have been prevented, the more agitated he became, and the more desperate he felt to escape into socializing, into the noise and distraction of other people's voices.

But avoidance had its own logic, one that tightened around him like a knot. Every time he stayed late at the station to avoid going home, every time he filled his schedule so completely that there was no space for silence, he was reinforcing the belief that his thoughts were genuinely dangerous, that the memory was something he couldn't survive alone. The constant socializing became its own kind of exposure: he'd be at a friend's house, someone would open a bottle of wine, and the smell would hit him before he could brace himself, catapulting him back into that warehouse. And now, trapped in a room full of people, he couldn't show his distress. He'd excuse himself to the bathroom, close his eyes, and wait for his heart to stop racing. The avoidance of hospitals and ambulances—the very spaces that defined his profession—had become impossible to maintain while still working. He'd started making excuses to stay off certain routes, to avoid the emergency department when dropping off patients. His colleagues had noticed. The respect that had taken three decades to build was beginning to fracture.

What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was a moment of clarity that terrified him more than the memories themselves. He realized he was becoming a stranger to his own life. His marriage was strained; his work performance was deteriorating; and the avoidance strategies that had seemed like survival had become their own kind of slow suffocation. He was sixty-one years old, and he was afraid that if he didn't find a way to break the cycle, he would lose everything he'd built—not to the chemical exposure, but to the architecture of his own escape.
